growth_story.headline: Bahrain's income per person slid through the 2000s, then crept up to a new high in 2025 on non-oil growth, just before regional conflict struck in 2026.
growth_story.arc: Since 1990 Bahrain's growth has run in three eras: income per person grew 3.2 percent a year in 1990–2000, fell 1.5 percent a year in 2001–2009, and grew 1.2 percent a year in 2010–2025. In the 2000s, building projects multiplied, foreign investment rose and Bahrain brought in many foreign workers, so the population grew sharply while income per person slid from 25,408 dollars in 2000 to 22,207 in 2009. Growth returned after 2010, but the 2014 fall in oil prices worsened the budget and external deficits, and the 2020 pandemic cut income per person by 5.2 percent. Non-oil activity, with financial services prominent, drove the recovery: income per person rose 4.8 percent in 2022, passed its 2000 level only in 2024, and reached a new peak of 26,592 dollars in 2025. That rise came alongside high and rising public debt, and conflict in the region in early 2026 cut oil output and exports.

threads.title: Imported labor, fast population growth
threads.text: From 2000 onward, foreign investment rose and large building projects multiplied, and Bahrain met the demand for labor by bringing in foreign workers. The population grew sharply, and income per person fell in most years from 2001 to 2009.

threads.title: Rising public debt
threads.text: Government debt kept rising through the recent recovery. In 2024 it passed the peak it reached in the 2020 recession, and it was higher still in 2025, with the government relying mostly on overdrafts from the central bank.

threads.title: Regional conflict in 2026
threads.text: Conflict in the Middle East in early 2026 restricted maritime traffic and hit Bahrain's oil sector and exports. The World Bank expects the economy to shrink in 2026, though non-oil sectors kept growing early in the year.

since_last_year.text: Growth was solid in 2025, and income per person reached a new high. Then conflict in the Middle East in early 2026 disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and damaged refining and aluminum plants. The World Bank now counts Bahrain among the hardest-hit Gulf economies and expects the economy to shrink in 2026. The data end in 2025, so they do not yet show this turn.

growth_story.tension: The sources describe the 2000s as a time of megaprojects, rising foreign investment and heavy hiring of foreign workers, yet income per person fell 1.5 percent a year over 2001–2009. The sources point to fast population growth driven by imported labor, but they do not say how much this weighed on income per person, and they do not explain the fall in full.
